doc.title: Buddy DeFranco interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

title: Glenn Miller's hits and the origin of 'Moonlight Serenade'
summary: From the Miller archives he recounts how 'Glenn's Theme' was written as a Schillinger exercise and Ray Noble turned down the clarinet-lead sound.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: And he was remarkable. Because it seemed like he really knew how to turn out hit records. He did. One after another. I can’t think of any other band that has as many hit recordings as Glenn Miller.
I guess it took him a while to find his sound but once he found it he really took it and ran with it.

Well actually it didn’t take him that long. I would go through the annals and the files of the Glenn Miller offices, and the archives, and I’d read scores of Glenn. Actually “Moonlight Serenade” was not “Moonlight Serenade” when he wrote it. He wrote it, he called it “Glenn’s Theme” and he wrote it as a graduation piece for Schillinger orchestration method and that was it. It was that lead clarinet with the saxes. And according to Dave Mackey, who was the executor for the Glenn Miller estate, he tried to sell that sound to Ray Noble, I don’t know if you’ve heard of Ray Noble, big band popular? And Ray Noble told him, not good, will never make it. But he just kept it until he got his own band, and he made it.
We should pair that guy with the people who turned down the Beatles I guess.
